newsitem.title: ITALY: Fiat profits slump as margins tumble.
newsitem.headline: Fiat profits slump as margins tumble.

text.p: Italian automotive giant Fiat reported a 36 percent slide in profits for the first nine months of 1996 on Monday as profit margins were squeezed hard while difficult market conditions showed little sign of improvement.

Italy's biggest private industrial group reported pretax profits in the nine months up to end-September fell to 1.759 trillion lire ($1.2 billion) from 2.743 trillion lire, while its overall turnover rose four percent to 57.918 trillion lire.

Fiat blamed the fall in profitability on the depressed Italian car market, the slow down in demand for industrial trucks and the effect that the high value of the lira had on exports from the Turin-based group.

It added that group nine-month operating profits slide to 1.706 trillion lire, equal to a profit margin of 2.9 percent, compared to 2.513 trillion lire, or 4.5 percent margin, in the first nine months of 1995.
"Clearly, profit margins are under great pressure. There is usually a seasonal drop in margins in the third quarter but this is a lot worse than expected," said one industry analyst.
He calculated that Fiat's profit margin had sunk to 1.1 percent in the third quarter (July-September) from 3.8 percent during the first half of 1996.
Fiat said that it had responsed to difficult market conditions by containing production, reducing stock level, increasing efficiency and reducing costs.
These factors had a negative impact on current results but should have a positive effect for the future, Fiat said.

The group's car division, Fiat Auto, recorded sales up 5.2 percent at 1.74 million cars in the nine month period, with sales to European nations outside Italy rising by 108,000, showing a rise in 24 percent in a ex-Italy European automotive market growing generally at around eight percent.
Fiat's truck division, Iveco, said sales of vehicle were up one percent to 86,700 trucks with its share of the European market rising two percentage points to 20.2 percent.

Its New Holland unit, which is the world's number one tractor maker and number two farm machinery group after U.S. John Deere, saw tractors sales down 3.7 percent at 61,400 with the group still trying to complete a full range of new models on the market while it suffered from a poor Brazilian market.

The group said that the nine-month results came before the sale of its fund management arm Prime to insurer Generali and the flotation of around 30 percent of New Holland on the New York stock market. Last year, results were boosted by the sale of Fiat's CEAC battery business for 380 billion lire.
The group added its cash flow in the nine month period slipped to 5.218 trillion lire from 5.843 trillion lire in the corresponding nine month period in 1995.

The results came out after the Milan stock market had closed where Fiat's shares closed down 3.36 percent at 4.378 lire in a slightly lower Milan market. This came after investment bank CS First Boston had downgraded its 1996 and 1997 earnings forecasts due to the depressed Italian car market and the high lira. ($1=1,512 lire)
